blogs.title: From ‘Right‑to‑Control’ to ‘Fraudulent‑Inducement’: How the Fifth Circuit Aligns with the Supreme Court’s New Fraud Paradigm
blogs.description: This post dissects the Fifth Circuit’s reliance on the Supreme Court’s recent decisions in *Ciminelli* and *Kousisis* to reject the district court’s “right‑to‑control” dismissal. It will explain the doctrinal shift away from requiring a traditional property interest toward a broader “fraudulent‑inducement” theory, outline the stare‑decisis analysis, and assess how this new framework will shape future securities‑fraud prosecutions, especially in the burgeoning social‑media influencer space.

blogs.title: The Indictment Standard Revisited: Why the Fifth Circuit’s De Novo Review Matters for Federal Fraud Cases
blogs.description: An examination of the Fifth Circuit’s approach to the sufficiency‑of‑indictment inquiry, focusing on its de‑novo review standard and the balance between protecting defendants’ double‑jeopardy rights and allowing the government to allege “scheme” and “intent” without concrete proof of victim loss. The article will compare this opinion to prior Fifth Circuit precedent and other circuits’ handling of the same issue, highlighting potential implications for plea negotiations and pre‑trial strategy.

blogs.title: Pump‑and‑Dump in the Age of Influencers: Expanding the Reach of 18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 and 1349
blogs.description: A sector‑focused analysis of how the Fifth Circuit’s decision embeds social‑media‑driven securities fraud within traditional wire‑fraud statutes. The blog will explore the statutory language, the court’s treatment of “material misrepresentation” on platforms like TikTok and Twitter, and the broader regulatory response, including SEC guidance and potential legislative reforms aimed at curbing influencer‑based market manipulation.

blogs.title: Victim Harm vs. Defendant Gain: Why Economic Loss Is No Longer a Prerequisite for Fraud Convictions
blogs.description: This piece delves into the Fifth Circuit’s affirmation that actual pecuniary loss to the victim is unnecessary under the fraudulent‑inducement theory, drawing on *Kousisis* and related case law. It will discuss the policy arguments for and against this expansion, consider how courts might assess “intent to obtain money or property” in practice, and speculate on the impact on defense tactics, including the use of “no‑loss” defenses in future securities‑fraud trials.
